• Common name: Fairy moss (also Mosquito fern, Water fern, Water velvet, Red water fern)
  • Scientific name: Azolla spp.
  • Difficulty: Easy to Medium
  • Lighting: Medium
  • Substrate: not needed
  • Placement in tank: floater
  • Growth rate: extremely fast
  • Fronds (leaves): up to about 1 cm
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed
  • Propagation: through spore formation or by splitting

Azolla is a genus of about 7 prolific, floating aquatic ferns in the family Salviniaceae. Two species are popular ornamental pond plants: Azolla filiculoides and Azolla cristata (formerly Azolla caroliniana). The genus is native to warm temperate and tropical regions of the Americas, from the southeastern United States to Central and South America, where the species are often regarded as weeds. It has been introduced to other parts of the world, including Asia, Australia and the United Kingdom.

Fairy moss is commonly found in shallow, still fresh waters (wetlands, ponds, ditches, lakes and streams), where it forms extensive intense green or reddish mats on the water surface. It is a miniature, short-stemmed, heterosporous fern with tiny green to reddish scale-like fronds that overlap each other, typically less than 1 cm long and covered in tiny epidermal protuberances called trichomes (unicellular in Azolla filiculoides, multicellular in Azolla cristata). It floats thanks to tiny gas bubbles in the fronds. Under full sunlight the fronds turn intense red.

The plant fixes atmospheric nitrogen through a symbiosis with the cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae, which lives in the cavity of the dorsal lobe of its leaf; phosphorus is the limiting nutrient for its growth. Its biomass can double every few days. It is rich in protein, amino acids, vitamins and minerals, can remove heavy metals such as copper, zinc, arsenic, lead, chromium, aluminium and nickel from water, and is used as a bio-fertilizer in paddy fields. Its dense mats prevent mosquitoes from laying eggs in the water, hence the name "mosquito fern".
Fairy moss can be grown in a freshwater tank of at least 40 litres. Larger tanks and ponds are more suitable because of its rapid growth and spreading ability once established.

• Vị trí: bèo dâu là cây thả nổi, không cần nền và không phải vùi hay buộc vào đâu cả. Muốn bèo chỉ nằm ở một phần bể thì dùng vật chắn khoanh nó lại.
  • Trước khi thả: chọn cây còn chồi và rễ rõ ràng. Bèo mua về có thể mang theo ốc hại, ấu trùng chuồn chuồn hoặc dính thuốc trừ sâu, thứ này cực độc với cá, tép và ốc. Vì vậy cần khử trùng bèo bằng dung dịch thuốc tẩy hoặc thuốc tím, tráng lại bằng nước đã khử clo rồi để khô tự nhiên.
  • Cách thả: rải từng cây con lên mặt nước. Giữ mặt nước êm và dòng chảy nhẹ, vì nước bị khuấy mạnh là lá thối.
  • Mấy tuần đầu: bèo đã bén thì lên rất nhanh và có thể phủ kín mặt bể. Khi đó cây bên dưới thiếu sáng, còn cá thì có thể bị ngạt do thiếu oxy. Dùng vợt vớt bớt chỗ mọc dày, dàn lại chỗ còn thưa và nhặt bỏ lá thối.

Care difficulty is easy to medium, because the plant grows and propagates so quickly that it needs regular thinning. Under optimal conditions the biomass can double in 4–7 days and dense mats can overrun the tank. Scoop out overgrowth with a net and discard it in a plastic bag; this also restores light to submerged plants. Remove decaying fronds from the mats to prevent oxygen depletion and water quality problems. Perform regular partial water changes and keep parameters at the ideal values.

Planting: spread individual plantlets on the water surface. Disinfect them first in a bleach or potassium permanganate solution, rinse in dechlorinated water and let them air-dry. Specimens should have well-defined shoot and root systems. You can confine the plant to part of the tank with a barrier, and thin out and redistribute very thick mats. Provide gentle water flow to prevent surface splashing.

Propagation:

  • sexually through spore formation (male and female spores: microspores and megaspores);
  • asexually by splitting or fragmentation of vegetative parts.

Problems:

  • Overcrowding: the plant can cover the whole surface in a short time, blocking light to submerged plants and significantly reducing oxygen, which can choke fish and other animals. Prune excess foliage frequently.
  • Leaf rot: often caused by strong surface agitation. Keep water movement slow or gentle.

Temperature: optimal 20–25 °C, but the plant tolerates 5 °C up to 45 °C. Cold (−4 °C and below) or prolonged freezing in winter makes the fern die back, often producing buds that sink to the bottom until spring.

pH: survives at pH 4.5–8.0; optimal growth at 6.0–7.5.

Hardness: thrives in soft to fairly hard water; in aquariums 4–18 dGH.

Brackish water: can grow in brackish water with low salinity (>8.4 g/l), but its tolerance to salinity has not been explored.

Lighting: strong light is required for optimal growth. In bright light and warm conditions growth is exponential and the fronds turn intense red; according to a study, reddening is a response to low temperature and high light and can be prevented by shading. Provide moderate to high light from good-quality LEDs with a photoperiod of 8–10 hours.

Flow: the fern comes from shallow, slow-moving water, so avoid strong surface agitation, which causes the fronds to rot.

Substrate: irrelevant, as the plant grows on the surface.

CO2 and nutrients: no CO2 is needed, since as a floater the plant gets enough from the air. Nutrient-rich water helps it grow vigorously; liquid fertilizers rich in phosphorus, iron and potassium encourage healthy growth and vivid colour. Very high nutrient levels make growth explode, and thick mats reduce oxygen levels, so aim for a middle ground.

Benefits:

  • Removes excess nutrients and heavy metals from the water; according to a study it can even remove low concentrations of copper.
  • Algae control: it reduces light below the surface and consumes excess nutrients.
  • Hiding place for shrimp and small fish.
  • Foraging place: it hosts biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Helps prevent fish from jumping when there is no lid, but beware of overgrowth.
  • Animal food: about 23.8% crude protein, usable as food for fish, shrimp, snails, crayfish and crabs. Blend it with montmorillonite clay as a binder, spread it thinly, let it dry completely, break it into small pieces and feed.

Tankmates: compatible with most common freshwater fish (zebra danios, rasboras, dwarf gouramis, mollies, Endlers, pygmy corydoras, platies, swordtails, otocinclus, killifish, royal farlowella, panda garra, white cloud mountain minnows, guppies, tetras), Neocaridina and Caridina shrimp, and snails (Japanese trapdoor, ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, chopstick, black devil, Asolene spixi, rabbit, white wizard snails). Choose species that tolerate shade or use the mats for spawning, shelter and feeding. Herbivorous or large fish such as koi, goldfish, Texas cichlids, Jack Dempsey, Red Devil and oscars may eat the soft foliage, but the fern withstands grazing and doubles its biomass every few days.

Shrimp tanks: high CO2 and copper (found in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Buying and quarantine: fairy moss can be bought at local fish stores, nurseries and online. Choose healthy, brightly coloured plants with intact shoots and roots. The plants can carry parasites, hitchhikers such as pest snails, or predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs), or may have been treated with pesticides that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates, so quarantine and disinfect them before use.

Interesting fact: scientists believe Azolla helped trigger an ice age: around 50 million years ago it covered the entire Arctic Ocean, taking up abundant nitrogen and carbon dioxide, and a succession of ice ages began once atmospheric CO2 dropped below 600 ppm around 2.6 million years ago.
